transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start off, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?

Yeah, uh… I guess what brings me in is I just can’t seem to sit still when I’m supposed to. It’s like there’s a little motor running under my skin, if that makes sense. Like in staff meetings at work, or even those briefings before church events—everybody’s sitting there listening, and I’m shifting around, tapping, standing up, looking for some reason to go check something or move a chair or whatever.

I mean, I’m a janitor, so moving around is kind of part of my day anyway, and I actually do better when I’m up doing something. But when I have to just sit there, I get real uncomfortable. Like I need to get up and do something, even if there’s nothing that needs doing.
Have you started or changed the dose of any new medications recently, especially any antipsychotic or anti-nausea drugs, around the time this restlessness began?

Um… I don’t think so? I mean, I’m not great at remembering the names of everything, but I haven’t started some big new medicine that I can think of.

Antipsychotic… I don’t think I’m on anything like that. Anti-nausea—no, I mean, I’ve had stomach bugs before, sure, and my wife keeps all kinds of stuff in the bathroom cabinet, but recently? I don’t think there’s been anything new or a dose change that lines up with this.
Thinking back, would you say you've felt this need to constantly move since you were a kid, or is this something that's only started more recently in your life?

Oh, no, this goes way back. I mean, I can remember grade school pretty clearly with that—I was always getting in trouble for popping up out of my seat, or talking before the teacher was done, or starting the worksheet before she’d even finished the directions.

My mom used to say I was “wound too tight,” which… I guess is kind of funny now, but back then I think she was tired. I’d be bouncing around while she was trying to get supper going, and then I’d be in trouble at school the next day for the same sort of thing. So yeah, it’s not just recent. It’s been there since I was a kid.
Do you often find yourself losing focus or drifting off mid-task—like starting a job and forgetting what you were doing, or losing track of instructions—even when you're not moving around?

Um… I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I know I’ll walk into a room and then think, “What did I come in here for?” but doesn’t everybody do that? My wife says I do it when I’m supposed to grab the trash bags and I come back with, like, a screwdriver because I saw the loose cabinet handle or something.

But if you mean just sitting there and my mind goes blank… I don’t know. It’s hard to separate it out, because I’m usually up doing something anyway. At work I’ve got my routine—bathrooms, floors, trash, all that—and if someone gives me a long list, I might need them to say it again, but… sorry, I’m kind of wandering. I guess I haven’t really paid attention to whether it’s losing focus or just me getting pulled toward the next thing.

Outside of situations where you can move around, like when you're reading paperwork, following written instructions, or doing quiet tasks at home, do you notice yourself making careless mistakes or losing your place because your attention drifts?

I’m not totally sure. Paperwork isn’t a big part of my day, so it’s hard to say. If I’m reading something with a lot of steps, I might go back and check it again, but I don’t know if that’s me losing my place or just wanting to make sure I didn’t miss something.

At home, quiet stuff… I don’t really sit with quiet tasks for long, honestly. I’ll start looking at a bill or some instructions and then—well, yesterday I was trying to figure out this thing for the sink, and then I remembered the garage light was flickering, so I ended up out there instead. But careless mistakes from my attention drifting? I don’t know. I haven’t really kept track of that.
Do you often find yourself interrupting or blurting things out before others finish speaking, or having trouble waiting your turn in conversations or lines?

Yeah… yeah, I do that. More than I probably realize.

Like if my supervisor starts telling me what needs done—“after you finish the bathrooms, go check…”—I’ll jump in with, “Oh, the break room trash?” before he’s even finished. And sometimes I’m right, but sometimes I’m wrong and then he has to stop and say, “No, that’s not what I was going to say.”

Same thing at church, if one of the staff is explaining where they want something cleaned or set up, I’ll kind of cut in because I think I know where they’re headed. I don’t mean to be rude. It’s just like my mouth gets there before they’re done talking. Then I feel dumb because they have to correct me.

Would you say these patterns of restlessness and interrupting have caused real problems for you—like conflicts at work, trouble in your marriage, or other difficulties—because of how they come across to people?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m getting in trouble every day, but it has caused some problems at work.

Like with room turnovers, when we’re trying to get things cleaned and reset fast, I’ll jump ahead because I think I know what they want, and then I miss part of what was actually said. Or with supplies—somebody’s explaining what to use or where to put something, and I cut in or make the decision too quick, and then it turns into friction. Not a huge fight, but people get irritated, and then I get irritated because I feel like they’re talking to me like I’m a kid.

My supervisor has had to correct me more lately. He actually suggested I talk to the employee assistance program, which… I don’t know, that kind of embarrassed me. I’ve been doing cleaning work a long time, so having someone basically say, “You need to get help with how you’re handling this,” that didn’t feel great. But yeah, I guess that means it’s become a real problem.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong (since grade school) pattern of hyperactivity (inability to sit still, internal restlessness, needing to move, fidgeting), impulsivity (interrupting supervisors and coworkers, blurting out answers before instructions finish), and some inattentive features (mind wandering off tasks, forgetting original purpose mid-task, needing repeated instructions). Symptoms are present across multiple settings (work, church, home) and have caused functional impairment (workplace conflict, supervisor referral to EAP, marital comments). Onset clearly predates age 12 per report of childhood school and home behavior. Medication-induced akathisia was ruled out (no recent antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure/dose change). Because both hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms are present and impairing, though inattentive symptoms are less clearly quantified, the combined presentation supports the combined type (F90.2) rather than a pure subtype.
